titleStmt.title: Computational positive psychology: advancing the science of wellbeing in the digital era

funder.orgName: Shenzhen Education Science Policy Research Project
National Natural Science Foundation of China

div.p: Positive psychology (PP) is in its third wave, evolving towards an interdisciplinary study of wellbeing. This article proposes computational positive psychology (CPP) as an emerging interdisciplinary field that integrates PP with computational science and technology to advance the understanding of wellbeing and develop evidence-based strategies to promote sustainable flourishing. The key features of CPP include addressing novel research questions that have received limited investigation in the existing literature, collecting large-scale and multimodal data, constructing computational models, and utilizing the results to advance theories, research, and the practice of wellbeing. We review CPP research topics such as: (1) advancing theoretical wellbeing models, (2) efficiently measuring wellbeing and positive traits, (3) exploring interdependent dynamics between individual and systemic wellbeing, (4) enhancing positive psychology interventions, and (5) improving collective wellbeing. The transformative potential of CPP for understanding and promoting wellbeing in the digital era is highlighted, and future research directions are discussed.

Seligman and Csikszentmihalyi (2000) (van Zyl et al., 2023) Yaden et al. (2018) Kern et al. (2020) Lomas et al. (2020) Wissing (2021) Positive psychology (PP) has made significant advancements and profoundly impacted the scientific study of wellbeing sincepublished their foundational paper 20 years ago. However, the field has also faced criticism regarding its theory and measurement, its focusing on the individual and western culture, and its isolation from mainstream psychology. Scholars have recognized the need for PP to evolve and have provided their ideas for improving it.introduced a range of technologies, including big-data methods, psychopharmacology, non-invasive brain stimulation, and virtual reality (VR), to enhance the capability of PP in more effectively measuring wellbeing and intervening to improve it.proposed systems informed positive psychology, which integrates principles and concepts from systems sciences, to facilitate the evolution of PP as a field that promotes both individual and collective wellbeing.identified the present stage of PP as the third wave that seeks to improve the complexity in research scope and methodologies of PP.further describes the third wave of PP as the beginning of a new domain of inter-or transdisciplinary wellbeing studies.

This paper begins with a contextual background for understanding the primary focus of CPP in advancing the field of PP and wellbeing science. We present our viewpoint on the challenges faced by PP and clarify the scope and role of CST in relation to CPP. Subsequently, we present an overview of CPP, delineating its key features and advancements compared to the traditional approach to PP. Furthermore, we review existing literature that has employed computational approaches to investigate PP and wellbeing, which serves as early exemplars of CPP. Finally, the potential future directions for CPP research and practice are discussed.

div.head: The challenges of positive psychology
div.p: (Rusk & Waters, 2013) Lambert et al., 2015) Linton et al., 2016) Diener et al., 2018) Agteren et al., 2021) Wellbeing is an appealing topic that has attracted the attention of scholars from various disciplines, including philosophy, economics, and psychology. PP is among the fastest-growing and most fruitful of these fields. Researchers in PP have examined such topics as theories, models, and concepts of wellbeing (e.g.; the measurement of wellbeing (e.g.; the antecedents and consequences of wellbeing (e.g., and how to improve wellbeing (e.g. van.

(Christopher & Hickinbottom, 2008) (Lomas, 2021) (Lambert et al., 2022) Smith et al., 2022) Despite making significant contributions, PP faces challenges in addressing the complexities of theory, methods, and practices that arise from an interconnected society in the digital era. The development of smartphones and other portable devices has enabled individuals to stay constantly connected online, where people with diverse backgrounds influence and are influenced by others in the pursuit of happiness, grounded in their value systems. This pervasive connectivity challenges established theories of wellbeing that have predominantly emerged from a Western individualistic context. Wellbeing has diverse meanings for various cultures, groups, and individuals, and its conceptualization carries substantial implications for mental health outcomes. Moreover, wellbeing may vary over time and across domains, even within a single individual. PP necessitates more sophisticated theories to comprehend the complexity of wellbeing experiences. Computational approaches, as we will elaborate further below, may offer novel perspectives and valuable insights into understanding individual and cultural differences in wellbeing (e.g..

(van Zyl et al., 2023) (Woo et al., 2023) Moreover, the evolving digital landscape poses methodological challenges for PP as individuals increasingly engage with digital devices, generating extensive psychological and behavioral data. This big data approach holds great promise for measuring wellbeing effectively and unobtrusively and understanding dynamic relations between individual and contextual factors. However, typical methods in PP have yet to effectively utilize these data due to a lack of advanced tools for rapidly collecting, storing, and processing the data. Leveraging computational methods to measure wellbeing through multimodal data could address the longstanding criticism of PP's reliance on subjective self-report measures. In addition, conventional PP methods have limited capacity to account for individual factors, contextual factors, and their interactions. Most existing research in PP adopts a variable-centered approach, which assumes that the variables function similarly across all individuals because they come from a single population. The gold standard randomized controlled trial method attempts to control for the effects of personal or contextual factors to reveal linear causal effects of the independent variable on wellbeing outcomes. Computational methods can analyze the non-linear dynamics among multiple factors, providing insights into the dynamics between individuals and their contexts.

(Waters et al., 2021) (Ciarrochi et al., 2016; Kern et al., 2020) (Goldstone & Janssen, 2005) Regarding practice, PP faces the challenge of expanding its conventional focus on individual wellbeing to encompass collective wellbeing. This challenge becomes particularly significant in light of the COVID-19 pandemic, which has elevated awareness of global interdependence. Addressing collective wellbeing, however, does not mean applying a one-size-fits-all approach. Instead, it adds a layer of complexity, requiring personalized, contextualized, and culturally sensitive strategies. Meeting the practical demands of a large population requires the development of cost-effective tools and personalized interventions applicable across various contexts. Incorporating computational technologies, such as artificial intelligence, for monitoring, intervention, and real-time feedback is an effective way to tailor interventions to individual needs while simultaneously enhancing wellbeing at the group, community, and population levels. Moreover, computational models of collective behavior may be used to advise organizational design or public policy.
Therefore, it is imperative for PP to incorporate computational approaches to navigate the complexities involved in investigating and enhancing wellbeing.

div.head: Roles of computational science and technology
div.p: The CST field encompasses a vast and diverse range of disciplines. In this article, we provide an overview of some relevant areas of CST that are closely aligned with the advancement of PP. By doing so, we aim to provide readers with a comprehensive understanding of the scope of the computational methods and techniques that are commonly employed in CPP today, and those that potentially will be employed in CPP in the future.

(Seligman et al., 2005) (Haeck et al., 2016) (Parks et al., 2012 (Parks et al., , 2018)) Liu et al., 2020) (Lyubomirsky & Kurtz, 2013) (Carissoli et al., 2015) Applying computers in research on PP is not new. Internet technology has been employed to facilitate data collection and the delivery of interventions in the field of psychological research since the dawn of the new millennium. Researchers have encouraged users to participate in empirically-verified PPIs (for example, that are focused on expressing gratitude or reflecting on one's best self) through websites. As smartphones and mobile computing gained popularity, investigators in the field of PP have begun to exploit mobile devices as conduits for delivering PPIs, analyzing physiological differences associated with various levels of subjective well-being (I., collecting data with the experience sampling methodor designing mobile applications dedicated to fostering meditation practices. However, these early stages primarily focused on the supportive role of computers and cellphones for data collection and intervention delivery and had limited utility to effect changes to underlying theories and methods of PP.

(Beutler et al., 1991) (Seligman, 2012) (Heintzelman et al., 2023; Proyer et al., 2015) Greer et al., 2019; Jeong & Breazeal, 2017) (Wang et al., 2022) (Baños et al., 2014) (Bell et al., 2020) Liu et al., 2024) (Demszky et al., 2023) 1 In recent years, the rapid development of CST has opened up the potential for fundamental theoretical changes and even paradigm shifts in PP and wellbeing research. Traditional psychological research has often focused on average effects, with less attention being given to individual differences. However, researchers have long advocated for a greater emphasis on matching individuals with appropriate psychological treatments. In PP research, where the conception of happiness varies greatly among individuals, a personalized approach is necessaryand studies have shown that providing personalized positive psychology exercise recommendations through recommendation systems can effectively enhance the effectiveness of psychological interventions. Technological advances have facilitated the development of innovative tools, including recommendation systems and chatbots, for personalized wellbeing interventions (e.g.. Another area of advancement includes VR, augmented reality (AR) and the metaverse. Despite VR being used in psychological interventions for a decade, recent advancements in sensors, machine learning algorithms, and game design have significantly enhanced the applicability of VR/AR in PP and wellbeing research. VR/AR helps increase the ecological validity of highly controlled environments, enhance personalization and engagement, and automatically track multimodal datasuch as participants' movements and heart ratethroughout the ongoing research process. These advantages enable VR/AR to serve as intervention tools and to facilitate assessment and research within the realm of CPP. Furthermore, recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) and artificial intelligence (AI) have significantly enhanced the data collection, analysis, and conversation generation capabilities of computers. PPIs enhanced by LLM-based chatbots have shown to effectively improve wellbeing (I.. Looking ahead, the collaboration between PP and CST holds great promise for transformative changes in the scientific study of wellbeingIn Figure, we provide an illustrative overview of the development of CST and its relationship with PP. Despite the substantial developments in CST over the past two decades and their contributions to PP, until recently, they have been used separately as instruments to measure psychological variables; there has limited integration or collaborating between these fields and PP to advance theoretical understanding or promote paradigm shifts. However, we are currently at the forefront of collaboration between the third wave of PP and the development of CST, and this has the potential to bring about transformative changes in the scientific study of wellbeing.
